newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS-Volvo on recovery road despite let-down.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Volvo on recovery road despite let-down.

text.p: Swedish automotive group AB Volvo posted below-par earnings for the first nine months of 1996 but said a total overhaul of the company that began in 1995 had put it on the road to recovery.

"We have focused on core business operations -- the divestment process is almost completed; we have full control of the strategic business operation; we have a strong balance sheet," chief executive Soren Gyll told a news conference.
But there is undoubtedly some way to go.

A 12 percent rise in pre-tax profit to 12.03 billion Swedish crowns ($1.83 billion) was entirely due to capital gains on share sales, including 7.77 billion crowns in revenue from the disposal of U.S.-Swedish drugs group Pharmacia & Upjohn Inc.
With analysts polled by Reuters predicting a nine-month pre-tax profit of 12.79 billion crowns, the share market was quick to punish the shortfall.
Volvo shares closed three crowns lower on the day at 138.
Sales fell 12 percent to 113.6 billion crowns, with truck sales sliding 14 percent to 32.71 billion crowns and car sales down five percent at 59.83 billion.

Operating profits from the core vehicles business slumped to 2.32 billion crowns. Despite a 600 million crown boost from currency movements this year, the figure was just over a quarter of the 8.84 billion crowns reported a year ago.
Nonetheless, Volvo's management said new models and a recovery on key markets would return the group to healthy profitability in the near term.
As foreshadowed by the group, Volvo Truck's performance was a major handicap, suffering from weak demand in North and South America, although European deliveries rose by six percent.
Volvo Truck president Karl-Erling Trogen said the group's new VN series had been well received in the make-or-break U.S. market, with orders for 1,500 trucks received to date.
"With the VN series and other efforts we are now making, we are sure of success in North America. We have great confidence in this," he told a news conference.

The fate of Volvo's car division is in the hands of a suite of new models. The popular 850 series saw an eight percent increase in sales, and Volvo said sales of the S40/V40 range launched earlier this year were "favourable".
The new C70 luxury coupe presented at the Paris car show earlier this month has yet to make its mark.

"Volvo Cars' income level is unsatisfactory but is developing positively," Gyll said. "This is an effect of the cost rationalisation measures implemented and increased revenues from the Volvo S40 and V40."
Analysts said the weak result from the truck unit, where operating profits fell to 413 million crowns from 4.03 billion a year earlier, was the most alarming feature of the report.
"Volvo Truck has in been the company's main profit generator throughout the early 1990s," said Bertil Nilsson of Sweden's Nordiska stockbrokers.
"The result was weaker than expected even though we already knew that that trucks would have to take heavy costs in the third quarter," he added.
Jan Ihrfeldt of Sweden's Foreningsbanken said the market had pinned its hopes on the truck division.
The only real bright spot in the report was that results of the car division were slightly stronger than expected.
"Cars did what was expected of them if not more. By increasing profit in the third quarter over the second, Volvo has shown that it is capable of earning money," John Lawson of Salomon Brothers said.
